steps.title: Preliminaries
steps.instruction: Imagine a decision-maker (DM) who faces the problem of choosing one attribute (or alternative) from a set of attributes (or alternatives). Let's denote this set by C, and c1, c2, … being the members of this set.

steps.title: Preliminaries
steps.instruction:
Definition 1
Ordinal relations
[10]

steps.title: Preliminaries
steps.instruction: Ordinal relation (also called order relation or preference relation) is asymmetric relation, i.e., there is no case where c1>c2 and c1<c2 are simultaneously possible. Thus, either c1≥c2 or c1≤c2.

steps.title: Preliminaries
steps.instruction: Definition 2Strict ordinal relations[9,10]

steps.title: Preliminaries
steps.instruction: A strict ordinal relation (>) is an ordinal relation that results in a strict linear ranking as determined by the weights (a ranking in which ties are not permissible), i.e., c1>c2 or c1 c2 and c2>c3, then c1>c3-Acyclicity: if c1>c2>c3>…>cn−1>cn, then if cn≠c1,

steps.instruction: In short, the strong ordinal relation implies:c1 is strongly preferred to c2 (or vice versa).

steps.title: Preliminaries
steps.instruction: Definition 3Weak ordinal relations[9,10]

steps.title: Preliminaries
steps.instruction: Strict ordinal relation where indifference is permissible is called weak ordinal relation (≥), whereas indifference is the absence of strict preference in either direction, i.e., c1≥c2 or c1≤c2. Thus, a weak ordinal relation is an ordinal relation that results in a weak linear ranking as determined by the weights (a ranking in which ties are allowed). In short, the weak ordinal relation encompasses two relations;c1 is weakly preferred to c2 (or vice versa) and c1 is indifferent to c2.

steps.title: Relationship between the OPA and OPA-S
steps.instruction: At this stage, a natural question may arise in the readers' minds: the original OPA follows strict ordinal relations or weak ordinal relations? This is the question largely left unanswered in the literature. Theorem 1 proves that the OPA and the OPA-S are two forms of the same model, and therefore, the original OPA follows strict ordinal relations.

steps.title: Relationship between the OPA and OPA-S
steps.instruction: Theorem 1The weights of the OPA-S (as presented in Eq. (13)) are equivalent to those obtained through the original OPA (as proposed by [1]).

steps.instruction: It should be noted that when r=1, the value (Wj′(r)−Wj″(r+1))−1n equals zero. Thus, we get Z′≤0 as the first constraint consistently, and since it's a maximization function the maximum value of Z′ is always 0. On the one hand, the maximizing objective function would not let Z′ become negative and on the other hand, even if Z′ gets a positive value, the model with the constraint Z′≤0 will not let it become positive. This constraint is important in determining the feasible region. The first constraint in the model (i.e., Z′=0) makes other constraints redundant in determining the optimum value of Z′. Therefore, replacing rZ′ with Z′ will not make any difference except bringing convenience in the modeling. steps.title: Relationship between the OPA and OPA-S
steps.instruction: Eq. (17) represents the OPA model of Ataei et al. [1]. Hence, Theorem 1 is proved. This revelation is no small contribution to the theory of multiple attribute decision-making, in general, and the Ordinal Priority Approach, in particular, for some reasons. For instance, Theorem 1 shows that the two models produce comparable weights of the attributes despite having different objective functions. The fact that two procedures yield a comparable set of weights validates the logic on which the OPA is built. To the best of our knowledge, there is no other MADM technique that exhibits this kind of characteristic. Since the objective function in the OPA-S is always zero (see Theorem 2), the theorem also reveals the difference value of the weights (Wj′(r)−Wj″(r+1)) in the OPA that is always a constant (1rn) thus allowing us to quantify the ordinal distance between the weights of the attributes following strict ordinal relations. Two other theorems directly flow from Theorem 1.

steps.title: Relationship between the OPA and OPA-S
steps.instruction: Theorem 2The objective function of the OPA-S is always zero.

steps.title: Relationship between the OPA and OPA-S
steps.instruction: Proof. The derivation of Eq. (15) from Eq. (14) proves it.

steps.title: Relationship between the OPA and OPA-S
steps.instruction: Theorem 3The OPA is more robust than the OPA-S.

steps.title: Relationship between the OPA and OPA-S
steps.instruction: Proof. It is proven from the literature [12] that the OPA model with a higher value objective function is more robust. Also, it is obvious from Theorem 1 that the objective function in the OPA has a higher value (positive value) than that of the OPA-S, whose objective function always equals zero. Therefore, the OPA is more robust than the OPA-S.

steps.title: Application
steps.instruction: Assume that there are three consumers, and we aim to model their choices based on the ordinal relations. Also, there are three choices for the consumers, Product A, Product B, and Product C. Each consumer replied as follows:Consumer 1: Product B is in fact better than Product A, and Product A is in fact better than Product C.Consumer 2: Product B is better (or almost better) than Product A, and Product A is better (or almost better) than Product C.Consumer 3: Product B is in fact better than Product A, and Product A is better (or almost better) than Product C.

steps.title: Application
steps.instruction: Considering the consumers’ opinions, we can express their choices as ordinal relations as follows:Consumer 1: Product B > Product A > Product CConsumer 2: Product B ≥ Product A ≥ Product CConsumer 3: Product B > Product A ≥ Product C
